slides.title: BEFORE WE BEGIN
slides.text:
Before we get started, I want you to understand why we’re here.

We’re here to become stronger as a club and closer as brothers and sisters.

What I’ve seen from BoneShakers this past year has been amazing. I’ve seen people come together in ways I haven’t seen before in my time as a member. I’m proud of that, and I want us to keep building on it.

First, I want to put everybody at ease. Nobody is here because they’re in trouble. I’m not mad at you, and the Board isn’t mad at you. That goes for everyone here today and everyone who takes this class in the future.

The Board and I have noticed some small things that keep coming up. As we talked about them, we had to take an honest look at ourselves. We realized we haven’t consistently given everyone the explanations and guidance they need.

That is a shortcoming on our part, and we own it. We made a mistake by assuming some things were understood instead of making sure we had explained them.

As your President, I share that responsibility. I can’t expect you to understand an expectation, the reason behind it, or how to follow it if we haven’t taken the time to walk you through it.

We owe you that. This training is one way we’re correcting our mistakes.

Going forward, every prospect will complete BSSC Foundations training before patching in as a full member. We want everyone to begin their membership with a clear understanding of the club and the support they need to succeed.

Today gives us a chance to step back, ask questions, and get our footing together. If something hasn’t been clear, I want you to feel comfortable saying so. Your questions will help us do a better job of leading this club.

Look at what we’ve already accomplished together. We just raised more than $20,000 through our charity concert effort. Could that become $30,000 or even $40,000 in the future? I believe we have that potential. Getting there takes all of us working together.

We need a strong Board that communicates clearly and supports its members. We need a strong membership that helps each other and follows through. Every person in this room has a part in making that happen.

I’m proud of this club. I’m proud of what we’re becoming. I want us to protect friendships, the brotherhood and sisterhood, and the good we can do together.

That’s why we’re here today: to learn together, strengthen our trust in one another, and take care of something bigger than any one of us.

slides.title: BEFORE WE GET STARTED
slides.text:
We have some useful information to cover today. If we all stay on task, we can stay on schedule and get the most out of the class. 

We have two planned 15-minute breaks for the restroom, a smoke, or stretching. 

Please return on time. While someone is speaking, hold side conversations until the break so everyone can hear. 

Silence your phone and keep it put away. If an urgent call comes in, step outside quietly. 

Pay attention, take notes if you like, and keep questions on the topic. 

We will also pause for questions throughout the class. If you need to step out before a break, do so quietly.

slides.title: BSSC FOUNDATIONS
slides.text:
Welcome to BSSC Foundations. Today I want to connect the pieces of being a BoneShaker: where we came from, what we stand for, and how we work together.

Some of you are prospecting, and some have already earned your cut. Wherever you are in that process, you should leave with a clearer understanding of the club and your place in it. Ask questions when something needs explaining. You do not need to memorize every detail today.

We will begin with our history, because our expectations make more sense when you understand the people and purpose behind them.

slides.title: OUR ROOTS
slides.text:
Our story begins with friendship and a love of riding. This picture takes us back to January 2005.

In the very middle is our very own Godfather Gordon, an original charter member who is still active in the club. He gives us a living connection to those early days.

Let’s look next at where those friends came together and how BoneShakers became a club of its own.

slides.title: OUR ROOTS
slides.text:
In 2005, about twelve friends came together at the original BoneShakers Saloon and formed BoneShakers Social Club. Riding and friendship brought them together. 

Helping people in the community became part of what they wanted to accomplish.

The saloon is an important part of our beginning, but the club had its own identity. A meeting place can change. The organization, its members, and its responsibilities continue.

We are carrying forward something people built together. Next, let’s talk about our founding President, Big John.

slides.title: OUR ROOTS
slides.text:
Our founding President was John Wilkerson, known as Big John. He helped bring the original group together and gave the club an early sense of direction.

The history handed down to us describes someone who cared about his community. Friendship and riding mattered, and so did using that shared interest to help local people and charities. Those priorities are still part of why we are here.

Remembering Big John helps us understand the responsibility that passes from one group of members to the next. We inherit the opportunity to enjoy this club and the responsibility to take care of it.

slides.title: OUR ROOTS
slides.text:
Big Lick is the name connected to our club logo, and its story starts with a tattoo John already had from his years in Roanoke. Roanoke was once known as Big Lick, a name associated with the area's natural salt deposits.

That tattoo became the starting point for the club's original logo. So when you hear us talk about Big Lick, you are hearing a connection to our beginning in 2005.

The workbench scene illustrates that origin story. On the next slide, you will see the original artwork alongside the later design, showing how that connection carried forward.

slides.title: OUR ROOTS
slides.text:
In 2025, BoneShakers reached its twentieth anniversary. The artwork on this slide connects that milestone to our beginning in 2005.

The original Big Lick and the renewed design look different, but they belong to the same club story. Twenty years together represents people showing up, friendships growing, leadership changing, and community work continuing.

An anniversary gives us a chance to appreciate that history and think about what we are handing to the next group of members. We honor the people who came before us through the way we represent the club and treat one another today.

slides.title: OUR ROOTS
slides.text:
The founders chose to build a Social Club. That identity gives us room for riders and nonriders, different backgrounds, and different ways of contributing.

You do not have to own a motorcycle to have a place here. You can enjoy the friendships, help at events, support community projects, and be someone other members can count on.

We want people to enjoy being BoneShakers. Clear expectations and dependable leadership help that happen because people know how things work and what they can expect from each other. Fellowship and good times belong alongside our responsibilities and the service we provide.

slides.title: OUR ROOTS
slides.text:
Giving back was part of the club's purpose from the beginning. People combined their time, contacts, and interest in riding to help local charities and people facing difficult circumstances.

Bikes for Tykes became an important part of that work, but our concern for the community reaches beyond one program. Sometimes we can provide money. Other times we can offer volunteer help, useful contacts, or support for another organization's effort.

The important connection is that we accomplish more by following through together. Our charitable work grows out of the relationships we build and the effort members are willing to share.

slides.title: GIVING BACK
slides.text:
Bikes for Tykes makes that purpose easy to see. Our 2026 goal is one hundred bicycles, one hundred helmets, and one hundred locks: eighty sets for the YMCA and twenty for Courthouse Horizons.

Each set represents a child and a family. Reaching that child takes much more than collecting a donation. Someone orders the bikes, receives them, assembles them, checks them, and gets them to the right place.

Members, donors, volunteers, and partners all contribute. That shared effort is something to take pride in, and it gives us a responsibility to protect the money and promises connected to the program.

slides.title: GIVING BACK
slides.text:
We would like to help every deserving person who comes to us, but we have to work within our resources and our approved budget.

We track the General Fund and Bikes for Tykes funds separately. A bank balance can include money reserved for bikes, existing obligations, or other planned expenses. The number in the account does not tell you how much we can freely spend.

Before making a financial commitment, we need the Treasurer's information and the proper approval. When money is unavailable, we can still consider other ways to help. Being responsible today protects our ability to keep helping tomorrow.

slides.title: OUR HISTORY AND PURPOSE
slides.text: Before we move on, what questions do you have about our history, our purpose, or the ways we give back? If something needs a clearer explanation, this is a good time to ask. Let’s take a couple of minutes, then we’ll talk about representing BoneShakers.

slides.title: REPRESENTING BSSC
slides.text:
When you wear our colors, people connect your actions with BoneShakers. They may never learn your name, but they will remember how someone wearing our patch treated them.

That includes a server, a donor, another rider, or a family at an event. Courtesy and good judgment strengthen the work every other member is doing. An argument or careless comment can affect people who were never involved.

Think about the club name you are carrying before you act. Looking out for our reputation begins with ordinary choices, and one of the most visible choices is how we wear and care for our colors.

slides.title: REPRESENTING BSSC
slides.text:
Every club-related patch has a purpose. Membership colors, sister patches, recognition patches, and ordinary merchandise do not all carry the same meaning or permissions.

Before adding a patch, changing its placement, or telling someone they can wear one, ask leadership. A gift or a well-meant suggestion does not automatically make a patch or placement approved.

You are responsible for understanding what you wear. You do not need every answer memorized, but you do need to ask before guessing. Keeping our appearance consistent shows respect for the club and for the people who earned the recognition those patches represent.

slides.title: REPRESENTING BSSC
slides.text:
Club-issued membership patches belong to BSSC. The club entrusts them to you to wear, and you must return them when our governing documents require it. Any approved exceptions for eligible Life Members and Past Presidents still apply. The vest itself and ordinary merchandise are separate from club-owned insignia.

When we are out representing the club together, put your cut on and keep it on. Do not drape it over a chair, leave it at a table, or expect someone else to watch it.

Keep your cut secure and take responsibility for it throughout the activity. Caring for it includes how it looks.

slides.title: How your cut looks matters
slides.text:
We have received criticism about the way some of our cuts looked. That is uncomfortable to hear, but it gives us a clear opportunity to improve.

Look at the comparison. Uneven placement, mismatched styles, and patches that appear careless create an impression about the whole organization. Clean material, secure stitching, and neat alignment show that we take pride in what we wear.

Before you go out, take a moment to look at your cut. If something needs attention, address it. Ask leadership before changing club-related patches. We want the care we put into our appearance to match the care we put into the club.

slides.title: REPRESENTING BSSC
slides.text:
BoneShakers is its own organization. We make decisions through our own governing documents and leadership, while also taking part in the wider motorcycle community.

Other clubs see how we ride, speak, and behave. Treat their members and Presidents with courtesy. If you visit an event, be a respectful guest and follow the directions of the people hosting it.

Enjoy building relationships, but bring official invitations, joint activities, and proposed commitments to our leadership. An individual member cannot promise BSSC's participation on everyone's behalf. Understanding who we are helps us represent ourselves accurately when we meet other organizations.

slides.title: UNDERSTANDING THE LETTERS
slides.text:
You will hear the letters MC, RC, and SC around the motorcycle community. MC stands for Motorcycle Club. RC stands for Riding Club. SC stands for Social Club.

Broadly speaking, an MC centers its identity on motorcycles and club membership. An RC usually emphasizes organized riding. An SC emphasizes fellowship and shared activities. Individual clubs have their own traditions and requirements, so those labels do not tell you everything about a group.

Our name is BoneShakers Social Club. Riding is important to many of us, and riders and nonriders both belong. Community service and friendship are central to our identity.

slides.title: OUR IDENTITY GOING FORWARD
slides.text:
Introduce us by our full name: BoneShakers Social Club. That tells a business, another club, or a prospective member who they are meeting.

Our identity brings together fellowship and community service, with riders and nonriders contributing side by side. We intend to carry that identity forward.

Members cannot independently rename BSSC, present us as an MC or RC, announce another BSSC chapter, or promise an affiliation. Questions about our local standing, another group's recognition, or future organizations belong with leadership. Bring those conversations to me rather than making statements or commitments for the club. Accurate introductions help us build respectful relationships.

slides.title: REPRESENTING BSSC
slides.text:
Over the last year, we have increased our presence with other clubs, and we have heard good comments about how we ride together and represent ourselves.

That progress comes from people showing up, following the ride plan, and treating others well. It belongs to the whole club. A positive experience with one member can make someone more comfortable supporting our next event or welcoming us back.

We should appreciate that progress and keep earning it. Relationships need continued care. The way we act at the next ride, meeting, or public event will help determine the impression we leave.

slides.title: REPRESENTING BSSC
slides.text:
When we are out together, people should see a club that handles itself with composure. Public arguments and insults can undo the good impression everyone else is trying to make.

If you disagree with a decision, use the club's process to raise it. Avoid turning a restaurant, event, or group chat into the place where an internal disagreement plays out.

Keeping ordinary club problems inside does not mean concealing misconduct or ignoring danger. Get appropriate help when needed. For routine concerns, bring the issue to the right person so it can be addressed with facts. That is where organized leadership matters.

slides.title: REPRESENTING BSSC
slides.text:
Internal discussions, disagreements, and members’ personal information deserve discretion. Do not share screenshots or repeat private club conversations outside the club. Bring routine concerns to club leadership through the proper process. Keeping club business private never means concealing misconduct, ignoring danger, or preventing someone from seeking appropriate help.

Example

A member of another club says, “You raised over $20,000 for Bikes for Tykes? That’s impressive! How did you get Elevation 27? Who’s your contact, and what kind of arrangement did they give you?”
It’s fine to celebrate our success and thank our supporters. Our private arrangements, fundraising plans, and business contacts stay within BoneShakers. Members have spent time building those relationships, and we respect that work by letting club leadership handle those conversations.

A friendly response:

“That event took a lot of teamwork, and we’re proud of what it means for the kids. Our President handles the partnerships and arrangements. You’re welcome to reach out to him.”

slides.title: REPRESENTING BONESHAKERS
slides.text: What questions do you have about wearing our patches, our identity as a Social Club, or how we represent BoneShakers? Let’s clear up anything that is uncertain before we move into the Board and leadership.

slides.title: HOW DECISIONS WORK
slides.text:
The Board helps turn our purpose into decisions the club can carry out responsibly. Directors review proposals, budgets, membership matters, and conduct concerns within the authority our rules provide.

They consider what the club can afford, who will do the work, and whether a proposal serves the organization. They make Board decisions together and record them so people can refer to what actually happened.

Our regular Board meeting is the last Tuesday of the month. Holiday scheduling, including December, may require an announced adjustment. Some decisions remain with the membership. Understanding how directors reach the Board helps explain that shared responsibility.

slides.title: HOW DECISIONS WORK
slides.text:
Eligible voting members elect directors for the announced open seats. The directors then choose the core officers through the officer-election process.

That means elected leadership comes through a process. A position carries duties to the whole club, including people who voted differently or see an issue another way. Directors need to prepare, use their judgment, and follow through.

Each director has one Board vote, even if that person holds more than one role. We keep the detailed election procedures in the governing documents. For today, remember the basic path: members choose directors, and the Board chooses the officers.

slides.title: HOW DECISIONS WORK
slides.text:
Leadership starts with learning the club. Under the ordinary eligibility rule, a person needs one completed year of active full membership before taking office on the Board. Prospect time does not count as that year.

A new director then spends the first-year learning Board responsibilities before becoming eligible for a core officer role. Prior completed Board service counts, and any authorized exception must follow the formal process.

Eligibility gives someone the opportunity to stand for a position. It does not guarantee election. These expectations give members time to understand how the club works before taking responsibility for leading it.

slides.title: HOW DECISIONS WORK
slides.text:
Two-year director terms allow experience to stay on the Board while seats come up for election. With staggered terms, the club can welcome new directors without having to start over with an entirely new group.

The number of open seats can change. Members should use the announced election information rather than assuming the same number of positions opens every year.

A Board seat and an officer assignment are different responsibilities. The governing documents and any approved transition determine their terms and eligibility. For members, the practical point is continuity: elections bring fresh involvement while experienced directors help carry unfinished work forward.

slides.title: WHO DOES WHAT
slides.text:
Every director has a working role. Directors review information, ask useful questions, disclose conflicts, and vote based on what serves the club.

The responsibility continues after a vote. If a director accepts an assignment, that work still needs to be completed and reported back. Good oversight includes checking that an approved decision turns into action.

Also remember that one director's opinion is not automatically an official Board decision. The club acts on decisions made through the proper process. With that distinction in mind, we can look at the officers who coordinate specific parts of the work.

slides.title: LEADERSHIP
slides.text:
The President coordinates the club's overall work. My responsibilities include chairing meetings, keeping officers connected, following through on approved decisions, and speaking for BSSC.

That means looking across the whole organization. A ride, a fundraiser, a membership question, and a community request may involve different people, but they still need consistent direction.

I use the authority of the office and the responsibilities the club has delegated. Decisions that require Board or membership approval still go through that process. When you are unsure where a club matter belongs, come to me so I can get it to the right person.

slides.title: WHO DOES WHAT
slides.text:
The Vice President works closely with the President to keep club business moving. That includes helping with orientation, checking progress, and following up when an assignment needs attention.

The role also provides continuity. If the President is temporarily unavailable, the Vice President carries out the duties provided in our governing documents.

Members should see the President and Vice President working together and giving consistent direction. If a question involves several people, that coordination helps us avoid missed work and conflicting answers. The next officer supports continuity in another important way: keeping an accurate record of what the club has done.

slides.title: WHO DOES WHAT
slides.text:
The Secretary keeps the club's official record. That includes meeting minutes, motions, votes, notices, and important membership and governing-document records.

When someone asks what the club approved, we should be able to find an answer in the record. That helps us avoid relying on a rumor or on several people's different memories.

You can help by giving the Secretary accurate information and reporting corrections promptly. Minutes capture the meeting's actions and decisions. Good records also help new officers pick up where previous officers left off. They protect the club's history and make our current work easier to follow.

slides.title: WHO DOES WHAT
slides.text:
The Treasurer keeps our financial information organized and accurate. The work includes receipts, deposits, account records, reports, budget preparation, and required financial filings.

Those records show what we have, what we owe, and which money belongs to a particular purpose. A healthy balance can still include funds that are restricted or already committed.

Members support that work by identifying payments clearly, keeping receipts, and turning money over promptly. Get the required approval before spending or promising club funds. Reliable records help the Board make responsible decisions and help us honor the trust members and donors place in us.

slides.title: WHO DOES WHAT
slides.text:
The Sergeant at Arms helps keep meetings and activities orderly and safe. That can mean settling a disruption, offering informal guidance, or responding when someone's behavior creates an immediate problem.

Cooperate with directions intended to restore order or protect people. Arguing about authority in the middle of a disruption makes it harder for everyone to resolve.

Immediate safety action and informal counseling are separate from a final disciplinary decision. Formal discipline follows the club's review process. The purpose of this role is to help people enjoy a safe, respectful club environment. That requires cooperation from all of us.

slides.title: LEADERSHIP
slides.text:
Now that we have covered the officers' responsibilities, here is what cooperation looks like in practice. When the President gives direction within the responsibilities of the office, members are expected to work with that direction.

If something is unclear, ask. If you disagree, use the established process to raise the concern. Publicly competing instructions or arguments can leave volunteers unsure which plan to follow.

Raise an immediate safety concern promptly. Required Board and membership approvals still apply. Clear direction helps a meeting or event run smoothly, and a clear review process gives people a way to address disagreements.

slides.title: LEADERSHIP
slides.text:
Respect for the office needs to continue beyond any one person's term. This applies to the person who follows me as President just as it applies while I am serving.

A strong club gives its next leaders accurate records, useful relationships, and members willing to work together. We should not have to rebuild those habits every time an office changes hands.

You can have your own views and still cooperate respectfully with the person carrying the responsibility. Supporting a good transition helps protect the friendships, events, and community work everyone enjoys. That also means learning how to disagree without dividing the club.

slides.title: LEADERSHIP
slides.text:
You are allowed to ask questions and disagree. What matters is how you handle the disagreement.

Explain the issue, give the facts you know, and say what outcome you are asking for. Keep the discussion about the problem. Insults, gossip, and attempts to recruit sides make a concern harder to resolve.

Give the responsible people an opportunity to review it. A serious complaint involving the President has its own reporting route, which we will cover later. Honest concerns should have a fair hearing. For an ordinary club question, the best starting point is a direct conversation with me.

slides.title: LEADERSHIP
slides.text:
When you have an ordinary club question and are unsure who should handle it, start with the President. You do not have to figure out the entire organization before asking.

I can involve the Board members as needed. Starting in one place helps us avoid several people giving partial answers or members receiving different versions of a decision.

If my answer does not resolve the concern, explain what remains unresolved and ask for Board review. We will cover that process shortly. You should also know where to find the written rules that guide those answers.

slides.title: COMMUNICATION AND RESPECT
slides.text:
If something in this club bothers you, bring it to me. Going from one brother or sister to another complaining, repeating rumors, or trying to get people on your side does not fix the problem. 

It creates sides and makes the issue harder to resolve. Bring me the facts, tell me what concerns you, and tell me what you are asking us to address. 

You can disagree and raise questions respectfully. Members can seek personal support, report misconduct, and raise concerns without retaliation. 

If the concern involves me, speak with the Vice President. If anyone is in immediate danger, get to safety and call 911.

slides.title: THE BOARD AND LEADERSHIP
slides.text:
What questions do you have about the Board, officer responsibilities, or where to bring a concern? 

We want you to understand how the club works and how to get an answer.

slides.title: TIME FOR A BREATHER
slides.text:
Let’s take a 15-minute break. You have time for the bathroom, a smoke, or a stretch. Please check the time now and be back in 15 minutes so we can continue together. 

When we return, we’ll cover our governing documents (bylaws) and shared standards.

slides.title: SHARED STANDARDS
slides.text:
Our governing documents give everyone a common reference. The bylaws explain the club's authority and members' rights. Operating Policies explain how procedures work. The Code of Conduct explains our expectations for behavior.

Prospects receive access when they become patched members. Once you have that access, read the current documents and ask about anything you do not understand.

You are not expected to quote every rule from memory. You are expected to know where the documents are, check them when needed, and follow what applies to you. Saying you did not memorize something does not remove that responsibility.

slides.title: SHARED STANDARDS
slides.text:
We are going to read the Code of Conduct together. Listen to the wording and think about what it means at a meeting, on a ride, online, or at an event. If something needs explaining, ask.

Acknowledging the Code means accepting responsibility for following it. We want everyone to understand those expectations and know how to get an answer when unsure. Here is what the Code asks of us.

Respect and Brotherhood/Sisterhood

Treat all members and associates respectfully and courteously, regardless of rank or status.
Uphold the values of loyalty, camaraderie, and trust within the club.
Resolve conflicts amicably and privately, seeking guidance from leadership if needed.
Respect differences in political, religious, and personal beliefs.
Harassment, discrimination, or bullying will not be tolerated.

Commitment and Participation

Strive to attend all scheduled meetings, rides, and events whenever possible. 80-85%
Actively participate in club activities and support charitable events and community outreach.
Represent the club proudly by wearing club colors/patches during official events.
Meet attendance expectations established in the club bylaws.

Lawful and Safe Riding

Always follow all traffic laws and ride safely to protect yourself and others.
Adhere to the club's riding formation and safety protocols during group rides.
Avoid reckless or irresponsible riding. – Over revving of engine after drinking and speeding!!
Remain quiet and attentive during all pre-ride briefings.
Do not operate a motorcycle while impaired by alcohol, illegal drugs, or medications that affect safe operation.

Confidentiality

Keep club business, votes, disciplinary matters, and other sensitive matters private.
Protect the club's reputation by refraining from gossip, slander, or defamation.

No Violence or Criminal Activity

Avoid engaging in violence, intimidation, illegal activities, or conduct that brings discredit upon the club.
Any violation may result in removal.

Chain of Command

Respect the club's leadership and follow their directives.
Bring grievances, concerns, or suggestions through the established chain of command.

Support for Members

Assist fellow members during illness, injury, funerals, family emergencies, roadside breakdowns, and other times of need.
Foster a supportive and inclusive environment.

Club Property and Colors

Treat all club property with respect.
Return all club-owned property when leaving.

Representation

Represent the club positively in public and online.
Avoid engaging in social media disputes, sharing internal club business publicly, or posting content that could harm the club's image.
Be respectful when posting photos or content involving fellow members.

Community Service

Members are encouraged to support charitable events and community outreach. Giving back is a defining value of the club.

Official Communications

Official club announcements will be made through approved communication channels. Members are responsible for staying informed.

Prospect Expectations

Prospects are expected to learn club customs, participate in club activities, demonstrate respect, and follow officer guidance.

Club Unity

Members shall not intentionally create unnecessary conflict, division, or hostility that negatively impacts the club.

That covers the written expectations. What would you like explained before we continue?

The next few slides apply those expectations to personal boundaries, privacy, and the way we handle a concern.

slides.title: SHARED STANDARDS
slides.text:
One important part of respect is honoring personal boundaries. If someone declines an advance, stop. Do not keep asking, send unwanted messages, touch them without permission, or make them uncomfortable for saying no.

This applies to members, guests, partners, staff, and people we meet at events. Alcohol does not excuse unwanted behavior. Someone should be able to enjoy being around the club without having to manage repeated pressure.

If you witness a concern, help the person get support and use the reporting process. Taking care of each other includes respecting a boundary the first time it is expressed.

slides.title: SHARED STANDARDS
slides.text:
Club information deserves careful handling. Member details, financial records, complaints, and internal decisions should stay with the people who have an authorized reason to receive them.

Before forwarding a message or screenshot, think about who is in it and whether you have permission to share it. Something sent privately can still end up in a public conversation.

Protecting confidentiality does not prevent good-faith reports to appropriate authorities, required disclosures, or confidential professional advice. It helps us handle ordinary club business responsibly and protect the people involved. When you are unsure whether information should be shared, ask first.

slides.title: SHARED STANDARDS
slides.text:
When leadership raises a concern, take it seriously and listen to what needs to be addressed. The person involved should have notice of the concern and a meaningful opportunity to respond.

A fair review considers the available facts, avoids conflicts of interest, and follows the governing process. A complaint needs examination, and immediate safety concerns may require action while that examination continues.

Cooperate with the review and understand any resulting decision, expectations, and available appeal route. Correcting a problem early helps protect everyone involved. The same need for fairness and clear decisions also explains why our meetings follow an organized process.

slides.title: OUR RULES AND CONDUCT
slides.text:
What questions do you have about our governing documents, personal boundaries, confidentiality, or how we handle conduct concerns? 

Please keep personal situations and names for a private conversation. Right now, let’s make sure the expectations and the process are clear.

slides.title: MEETINGS
slides.text:
Robert's Rules gives groups a shared way to conduct business. Henry Martyn Robert, an Army officer, developed the guide after struggling to lead a meeting. The first edition appeared in 1876.

For our purposes, the idea is straightforward: people take turns, discuss the actual question, and reach a clear decision. Everyone should be able to follow what the group is deciding.

You do not need to master parliamentary language for this class. Our governing documents take priority where they specify a procedure. What we need from members is attention, patience, and a willingness to let the meeting move in an orderly way.

slides.title: MEETINGS
slides.text:
During a meeting, face the speaker and keep side conversations down. If you are talking over someone, the people around you may miss information they need.

Use the chair's process to ask a question or raise a proposal. Explain what you want the club to consider, and keep discussion focused on that question. When a vote is required, the proper voters decide and the result goes into the record.

A personal concern that does not belong in the group discussion can be raised privately afterward. This helps the meeting stay useful while still giving people a way to get an answer.

slides.title: COMMUNICATION
slides.text:
If an ordinary concern remains unresolved, you can request Board review through the President. Tell me what happened, what remains unanswered, and what you are asking the Board to consider.

A clear request gives directors something they can evaluate. Bring relevant information and explain the outcome you want. Avoid turning the matter into a running argument in GroupMe or a campaign for people to take sides.

The Board will consider the issue within its authority and the governing process. A complaint involving the President uses a separate route so the person named in the complaint does not control their own review.

slides.title: COMMUNICATION
slides.text:
For an ordinary complaint, come to the President through the established process. Give specific facts and any available evidence so the concern can be addressed responsibly.

If the complaint involves the President, bring it to the Vice President for the full Board's attention. If that person is also involved, use an unconflicted director. Protect the privacy of the people concerned and avoid spreading the story around the club.

Retaliation for a good-faith report is unacceptable. If there is immediate danger, get appropriate help promptly. Respect for leadership includes having a fair way to raise a serious concern about leadership itself.

slides.title: COMMUNICATION
slides.text:
GroupMe, official email, and our approved announcements help us keep people informed. Read the whole message before replying, including the date, time, location, and any instructions.

When someone asks for a response, answer so the organizer can plan. If your availability changes, let the right person know. Do not assume another member will repeat every announcement or remind you personally.

Keep unrelated conversation from burying important event details. Take personal disagreements to a direct conversation or the proper review process. Staying informed is a shared responsibility, and a little attention saves volunteers a lot of unnecessary follow-up.

slides.title: COMMUNICATION
slides.text:
If someone criticizes BSSC on Facebook or elsewhere online, pause before responding. Send me the link or a screenshot so leadership can decide whether an official response is needed.

A comment can travel far beyond the people who originally saw it. Screenshots may leave out the context, and personal posts can still be connected to the club's name you wear.

Do not share confidential business or make promises for BSSC in a comment thread. You can protect the club by getting information to the right person and allowing the authorized spokesperson to handle the response. Let us practice that choice.

slides.title: LET’S TALK
slides.text:
Here is the situation: someone criticizes BoneShakers online, and a member starts arguing in the comments. What should happen next?

Think about what protects the club's reputation and what might make the situation harder to resolve. Who needs the information, and who has authority to respond for BSSC?

The useful next step is to stop adding public comments, capture the link or screenshot, and send it to leadership. That gives us a chance to review the facts and choose a response. The goal is to protect our name and relationships while getting the concern handled.

slides.title: BELONGING AND PARTICIPATION
slides.text:
Prospecting gives a person time to learn the club and gives the club time to get to know that person. Participation, respectful behavior, and completing the admission process all matter.

A sponsor should make introductions, explain expectations, and help the prospect find ways to take part. Prospects should ask questions and follow through rather than waiting for someone to explain everything twice.

After full membership, the responsibilities continue. Keep contact details current, complete required renewal paperwork and acknowledgments, and meet dues requirements unless an approved exemption applies. Earning the cut begins an ongoing commitment to the club.

slides.title: STAYING CONNECTED
slides.text:
Hangarounds have no internal club communications access. 

After signing up as a prospect, we add you to GroupMe. 

Fully patched members also qualify for the private Facebook group and approved member website access. 

Public Facebook remains visible to everyone.

slides.title: STAYING CONNECTED
slides.text:
The public account is Boneshakers SC, at facebook.com/boneshakers.sc.  - Anyone can follow it.

The BSSC Members Only Facebook group is for fully patched members. Anyone may submit a request, but full membership is required for approval.

slides.title: STAYING CONNECTED
slides.text:
Start at https://boneshakerssocialclub.com and click the person icon in the upper-right corner. Choose Sign in for an existing account or Create account for a new one. Complete the form and submit. Allow a few minutes for the automatic activation email. Click Activate account and set a password. Creating an account does not by itself grant private-page access. Approval is for full members. Once approved and signed in, open More to show the member pages.
Direct sign-in / signup: https://boneshakerssocialclub.com/m/login

slides.title: BELONGING AND PARTICIPATION
slides.text:
Participation keeps members connected and helps share the work. Know the requirements for your membership status and check your attendance record during the year.

If an event or meeting is missing from your record, raise it promptly while the details are easy to confirm. Waiting until the end of the year makes corrections harder.

Work, health, and family circumstances can affect anyone. If you are having difficulty participating, talk to me early so we can use the appropriate hardship review process. Different membership statuses have different requirements, and anyone holding an assigned role still needs to carry out that role's responsibilities.

slides.title: BELONGING AND PARTICIPATION
slides.text:
People contribute in different ways. Someone who cannot lift bicycles may be excellent at welcoming guests, making calls, checking people in, or organizing records.

If you need an adjustment or help finding a suitable task, speak with me privately. We can do more when we match the work to the person rather than assuming everyone can do the same thing.

Our Good Will Ambassador helps people feel welcome and connects guests and newer members with the right person. Every member can help by making an introduction and including someone who is standing on the edge of the group. That sense of belonging matters.

slides.title: MEMBERSHIP AND PARTICIPATION
slides.text:
What questions do you have about prospecting, sponsor responsibilities, member access, or participation? 

If you are unsure what applies to you, please ask. We want everyone to know where they belong and how to get help. Next, we’ll cover riding together safely.

slides.title: RIDING TOGETHER
slides.text:
The Road Captain organizes the plan for a group ride. That includes the route, timing, stops, and the information riders need before departure.

Pay attention during the briefing. Understand the formation, signals, regrouping plan, and what to do if the route changes. Asking before we leave is much easier than trying to work something out while moving.

The Road Captain coordinates the ride with the Tail Gunner and other assigned support. Each rider still controls their own motorcycle and remains responsible for following traffic laws and riding within their ability. A clear plan works when the group understands and follows it.

slides.title: RIDING TOGETHER
slides.text:
The Tail Gunner takes the assigned rear position and helps the Road Captain know what is happening behind the group. That may include separation, a stopped rider, or a breakdown.

Know who is filling the role before departure. Listen to the assistance plan and understand how you should communicate if you need to stop or leave.

The Tail Gunner helps coordinate a response but cannot automatically see or solve every problem. Unexpected moves make the job harder and can put people at risk. Use the agreed signals and plan so the group has a chance to respond safely.

slides.title: RIDING TOGETHER
slides.text:
The pre-ride briefing deserves everyone’s attention. Stop side conversations and listen, even if you have ridden the route before. Know the destination, planned stops, regrouping plan, signals, and safe way to leave the ride. Ask questions before departure.

We ride single file and maintain steady, consistent spacing. Stay aware of the motorcycle ahead and the riders behind you. Avoid unnecessary gaps that stretch out the group, while keeping enough distance to brake, react, and maneuver safely. Maintain at least a two-second following distance and increase it for poor visibility, wet roads, or other hazards.

Ride smoothly and predictably. Avoid sudden acceleration, unnecessary braking, showing off, or pressuring another rider. The ride leader should set a manageable pace so the group can stay together safely.

If a vehicle enters the group, give it room and rebuild the formation when safe. If you become separated, follow the agreed regrouping plan. Never race to catch up or take a risk just to keep the group together.

A disciplined group earns respect through preparation, control, and good judgment.

slides.title: RIDING TOGETHER
slides.text:
Before drinking, decide how you are getting home. If someone is impaired, riding or driving is not a safe option.

Look out for each other. Help arrange another way home and involve the appropriate ride or club leadership. Keep the conversation respectful but take the concern seriously. An awkward conversation is worth having when someone's safety is involved.

Here is a situation to consider: a member has had too much to drink and insists they are fine to ride. 

Accepting help and stepping in for a friend are both part of taking care of the group.

slides.title: RIDING AND SAFETY
slides.text:
What questions do you have about the Road Captain, Tail Gunner, ride briefings, or getting home safely? 

Ask now if something would help you feel more confident on a club ride.

slides.title: TIME FOR A BREATHER
slides.text: We’ll take another 15-minute break now. Please check the time and be back in 15 minutes. When we return, we’ll talk about event responsibilities, our community partners, approvals, and taking care of the club’s resources.

slides.title: WORKING TOGETHER
slides.text:
An event runs well when people know their assignments before the crowd arrives. Ticket sales, merchandise, raffles, prize release, setup, and breakdown each need clear responsibility.

Know your assigned arrival time and check in with the coordinator. Setup access and volunteer reporting times may be different, so use the instructions for your role rather than assuming an earlier arrival is always useful.

Find out where your supplies are, what the job involves, and who handles questions. Ask before taking over a station or changing a process. Clear directions help volunteers succeed and keep a small misunderstanding from becoming an event-wide problem.

slides.title: WORKING TOGETHER
slides.text:
When you accept an event assignment, other people plan around that commitment. Arrive at the agreed time, check in, and be ready to do the work you accepted.

If you need to leave or step away, tell the coordinator and arrange relief. Do not assume another volunteer will notice an empty station and take over. Make a clear handoff of money, keys, supplies, and any unfinished work.

Stay through the portion of setup or breakdown you agreed to cover. If circumstances change, communicate early. Dependability makes volunteering less stressful and shows respect for the people giving their time beside you.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
Our donors and community partners help us accomplish things we could not manage alone. Their experience with us influences whether they want to help again.

Thank people, honor the agreements we have made, and give credit accurately. If someone asks about a sponsorship benefit, a donation, or official club participation, take the request to leadership before promising anything.

Direct official media questions and public statements to me as President. A friendly conversation can build a relationship without committing the whole club. We want our partners to know that when BSSC makes an approved promise, they can rely on us to follow through.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
Support comes in more forms than money. When someone provides space or services without charging us, that is called in-kind support.
AJ Gator’s gives us a place to call home. They earn business when we visit, and they also open early when needed and provide our meeting space at no charge.
Princess Anne Courthouse Volunteer Rescue Squad gives us a quiet, private, clean place for Board meetings every last Tuesday of the month. Those contributions help our club operate, even though no check changes hands.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
We return our partners’ kindness by showing up for them. We sponsored a hole at Princess Anne Courthouse Volunteer Rescue Squad’s annual golf tournament, supporting an organization that gives us meeting space every month.
Al and Steve gave their time to represent BoneShakers, and James stopped by too. We also partner with the squad at Christmas for the bikes.
When members take part, they help keep these relationships strong. Giving your time can be an important way to support the club and the people who support us.

slides.title: EVENTS AND COMMUNITY PARTNERS
slides.text: What questions do you have about event assignments, following through on a volunteer commitment, or supporting our community partners? Their support takes many forms, and our time and participation help us return that kindness. Let’s clear up any questions before we discuss proposals and approvals.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
If you have an event or fundraising idea, bring me a simple plan. Tell me who benefits, when and where it would happen, what it might cost, and who would do the work.

Send the request directly to me. A discussion in the main GroupMe thread does not mean the Board has reviewed or approved a proposal. Get a clear answer before contacting partners or making commitments.

A useful plan gives us a chance to consider the idea responsibly and explain any changes needed. Before discussing official approvals further, let us separate those proposals from the personal get-togethers we want members to enjoy.

slides.title: FRIENDSHIP AND FELLOWSHIP
slides.text:
Please spend time together outside scheduled club business. Invite members to your home for dinner, a cookout, a birthday, or an evening with friends. That kind of fellowship strengthens the club.

A personal invitation does not need to become a Board project. Make it clear that you are inviting friends in your own capacity.

If you want to present the gathering as an official BSSC event, raise money for the club, make club commitments, or produce invitations or items carrying our name or logos, get Board approval first. Personal hospitality is encouraged. Official use of the club's identity carries additional responsibility.

slides.title: BOARD APPROVAL
slides.text:
An official BoneShakers event needs Board approval before anyone announces, advertises, books, or promises it. That includes fundraisers and joint activities involving another club.

Bring the proposal through me so the Board can consider the purpose, resources, and commitments. Do not promise that BSSC will cohost, sponsor, donate, provide volunteers, or attend officially before that decision.

You can enjoy another group's event personally without gaining authority to commit our club. Be clear about the capacity in which you are speaking. Also remember that approving an event does not automatically approve every printed piece or item connected to it.

slides.title: PRINTING AND MERCHANDISE
slides.text:
The final design needs approval as well as the event itself. Before producing club-branded material, bring the proof and intended use through me for Board approval.

This includes printed and electronic flyers, forms, signs, tickets, banners, shirts, patches, mugs, and other items. Paying for it personally, giving it away, or making only one does not remove that requirement.

Use the approved artwork and wording. Do not redraw a logo, add an unapproved slogan, or send a changed design to a printer. If the design or use changes, get the revision approved before production or distribution. That protects a consistent club identity.

slides.title: OUR NAME AND ARTWORK
slides.text:
The BoneShakers Social Club name, Big Lick logo, and Bikes for Tykes logo belong to the club. They identify our organization and the work people trust us to carry out.

Membership does not give anyone personal ownership or unlimited permission to reproduce them. The Board controls authorized use, and a printer or vendor should receive club artwork only for an approved purpose.

Think about what happens when someone sees our name on a flyer, shirt, or donation request. They may reasonably believe the club stands behind it. Approval helps us protect that trust, keep our identity consistent, and avoid promises we never agreed to make.

slides.title: EVENTS, APPROVALS AND ARTWORK
slides.text: What questions do you have about getting members together personally, proposing an official club event, or using the club’s name and artwork? If you are unsure whether something needs approval, ask before making a commitment or producing an item. Let’s make sure that distinction is clear.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
We have covered how proposals receive approval. Now let us talk about why we are careful about how much fundraising we take on.

In earlier years, support came through several activities, including the October fundraiser, July poker run, golf and Pink Ride raffles, and partner events. Those efforts took real work and brought in money.

One earlier comparison recorded $1,767.90 from four smaller Bikes for Tykes activities and $6,628.44 from the July poker run and October fundraiser combined. Those were revenue figures, with incomplete individual cost comparisons. We also need to consider repeated requests for members' time, travel, tickets, and donated items.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
Our goal is to focus the main working effort and broaden the support around it. That gives members more room to enjoy fellowship and riding while still accomplishing meaningful community work.

Outside donors, sponsors, partner activities, and public attendance can help carry the campaign. We should not rely on the same members to buy every ticket and provide every donation.

The combined 2026 campaign passed twenty thousand dollars through the main concert, advance support, partner activities, and donations. That describes the wider campaign, rather than concert-day receipts alone. Clear assignments and wider community involvement help turn that support into a manageable effort.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
When you handle club money or prizes, use the approved process and keep a clear record. Know the prices, payment method, and correct place for each collection before starting.

Merchandise sales and donations need the appropriate records. For raffles, follow the announced rules and prize-release process. Do not add a drawing, change a prize, or create a new arrangement at the table on your own.

If something is recorded incorrectly or you are unsure what to do, tell me promptly so I can involve the coordinator and Treasurer. Reporting an honest mistake early makes it easier to correct and protects everyone involved.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND SERVICE
slides.text:
When someone asks the club for financial help, bring the need and proposed beneficiary to me through the approved process. Keep the person's circumstances private while the request is considered.

The Treasurer checks available resources, existing commitments, and any restrictions on the money. The Board considers the request under our rules. A deserving situation still needs that review before anyone promises assistance.

Compassion and responsible budgeting need to work together. We must consider the person asking for help while honoring commitments already made to donors, families, and club programs. If money is unavailable, we can consider whether another form of support would help.

slides.title: WORKING TOGETHER
slides.text:
Club equipment, supplies, records, and access belong to the organization. If you borrow or take responsibility for something, coordinate the use and make sure the right person knows where it is.

Return items promptly and ready for the next volunteer. Report damage, missing pieces, or shortages instead of leaving someone else to discover them during an event.

Good handoffs matter when roles change, too. Keys, records, equipment, and necessary access need to reach the next responsible person. The care we take with shared resources saves money and helps the next member do their job. Let us put these expectations into practice.

slides.title: FUNDRAISING AND CLUB RESOURCES
slides.text: What questions do you have about fundraising, handling money, requests for assistance, or caring for club property? You do not need to remember every procedure today, but you should know to ask before acting when you are unsure. Next, we’ll put some of this into practice.

slides.title: LET’S TALK
slides.text:
Let us try three everyday situations.

First, you need to leave an event before your volunteer assignment ends. Second, a business asks you to promise official club support. Third, you disagree with a decision made during an activity. What is your next step in each case?

For the first, contact the coordinator and arrange relief and a proper handoff. For the second, bring the request to the person with authority before making a promise. For the third, raise the concern respectfully through the established process. Clear communication and follow-through connect all three situations.

slides.title: BRINGING IT HOME
slides.text:
We have covered our history and many of the responsibilities that help the club function. Before we finish, think about why you joined and what makes you want to stay.

Is it the friendships, the rides, the chance to help someone, or having people you can count on? I would like to hear a few answers.

Those are the parts of the club we are trying to protect. Clear leadership, fair processes, dependable volunteers, and respectful behavior help make that experience possible. Each member contributes to whether BoneShakers feels like a place people are glad to belong.

slides.title: BRINGING IT HOME
slides.text:
I want BoneShakers to remain strong, welcoming, and enjoyable long after any one person's term ends. That depends on how we treat each other and how well we follow through.

Respect the people carrying leadership responsibilities. Ask questions through the right channel, take care of our reputation and property, and look out for members who need support. Make room for others to contribute.

Enjoy the friendships, rides, and community work that brought us together. We have a history worth knowing and a future we help shape through our own actions. Thank you for being part of it. What questions can I answer before we finish?

slides.title: BEFORE WE FINISH
slides.text: Before we finish, what questions do you still have? Let’s also return to anything we set aside earlier. I want you to leave knowing where to find an answer and feeling comfortable asking for help. Thank you for taking the time to strengthen our club together.
